Louder, Pierre!
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention to the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona that last night, he spoke very loudly.

He was alone, by the way.
Summer Recess

I was saying that I am sorry that the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition said to us in this House tonight that he would like to sit between 6 and 8 p.m., instead of letting everybody out for dinner, as yesterday this same leader did not return until 8.20 and consequently the debate had to be postponed for 45 minutes. I think one should not go too far in pretending that everybody is cheated as far as the right to speak is concerned in this House. Let us not exaggerate. I feel I ought to emphasize that during the work of the committee, those poor Liberal members have to put up for long hours with the silly rethoric of the opposition parties, and after that they claim they are not given the opportunity to speak in this honourable House. Therefore, I think it is about time we become serious. Now if the government has decided that it is time for members to go home to their ridings, it is because their constituents have needs and this is a fact the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition should be aware of, as well as members of the New Democratic Party. The best advice I can now give Progressive Conservative members is to return to their constituencies and ask people what they think of the present leadership of their party. What do they think of what they are doing in the House at this time? Do they think they are doing anything constructive to develop their country? They will soon realize that apart from destroying a few ideas, from boycotting in a very childish and disorderly way, this way of abusing the openness of the parliamentary system of the English-speaking world, only stems from a lack of leadership which is rubbing off on the members who are supposed to work for the people.
As a representative of one particular region, I cannot accept that. I want to say something. The day I have reached that point I want my colleagues and my constituents to say to me: Pierre, stay home, we do not need you to go and cry in Ottawa.
1 came here with the purpose of building not destroying and, especially not to waste the time of those who want to work.
One thing I hope, Mr. Speaker, is that the light of understanding shine on everyone. This applies also to the New Democratic Party. Listen, gentlemen of the No Decision Party, there is a limit to going from left to right, from one side to another, to changing one's mind from one day to the other. That can do for a while, but then it becomes hijacking because we do not know what the party line is, if one indeed remains. At one point, one did not know whether the NDP was more concerned about-I was going to say El Salvador, not Labrador, that is too close to us, they are not concerned about those kinds of things-about El Salvador than the economy of our country. Other times, other issues, they change their minds almost every day.
Beside, it is of the utmost importance that this party should establish a party line because it means a lot to all the Canadian people; this is what makes a healthy democracy and it has never been anything else but that. And how can you explain that this government, the government of the Liberal Party of Canada has been in power for such a long time in this

July 17, 1981
Summer Recess
country? It is because this party has based all its policies on one premise, that is individual rights and freedoms and free access of the riches of this country to every Canadian, not just' one class of Canadian, not just one generation of Canadians, not just one kind of Canadian but to all Canadians. But they will never understand that, that is impossible.
Mr. Speaker, when a party leader or when members are just the messengers of provincial premiers, where is that political party going if it is not to total destruction and this is forthcoming. And I say to my Progressive Conservative colleagues: Wake up because tomorrow you will be divided into ten parties with ten premiers to guide you. And you will then be facing a great and strong Liberal Party with a strong leader who is now going to lead the seven most powerful nations of the world into discussions with a view to achieving the security of the riches of this world so that everyone on this earth could share in them. Whatever those foot draggers may think, whatever the members of the Permanently Constipated Party may think-
Mr. Speaker, whatever the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Gimai-el) has been smoking, I think he should pass it around the House.
Order!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I am sure the hon. member, after reflection, would like to withdraw those remarks.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, I will be happy to withdraw those remarks. This is the most enthusiasm I have seen in the Liberal party in a year and a half, and I congratulate the hon. member.
Hear, hear!

This has been an interesting session; a session when there has been tragedy in this country. The tragedy is that gas prices have risen from $1.07 to $1.60 when, in the last campaign, it was promised that they would be kept down. Interest rates have gone from 14 per cent to 20 per cent. Inflation has risen from 9.5 per cent to 12.8 per cent, which is the highest in modern times, and the dollar has fallen from 86 cents to 83 cents and below, as compared with the American dollar.
Probably the most positive thing that has happened in this session is that the Attorney General was awarded an honorary doctorate of law. That is about the most positive thing we can say about this entire session.
As a relatively new member of the House of Commons, I am very disappointed that the government keeps bringing in closure on important issues. It invoked closure on the Constitution. As the member for Brampton-Georgetown, I was unable to speak on that bill because of closure. Then it brought in closure on energy issues and now it has brought in closure because it wants to go on holidays. It is shameful, Mr. Speaker.
I listened to the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) and I listened to the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean and others telling me that that they have to go back to their ridings to listen to the people. I do not know where they have been for the last year and a half but when they get back to their ridings, they are going to get an earful. I have been going back to my riding every weekend to listen to what the people have to say.
That party over there is in a lot of trouble. If I belonged to it, I would not go back to my riding; I would stay in Ottawa.
I get great enjoyment from some of the pontifications and lectures from the other side, Mr. Speaker. Today we heard about how we opposed everything. That is not true, Mr. Speaker. We have supported good legislation. 1 have seen many bills get three readings in this House in a matter of an hour because it was good legislation and we were able to support it.
We oppose those things that are wrong for this country and we amend those bills that we feel we can make better. That arrogant government opposite does not listen but rams things through. If things do not go its way, then it wants to close the House down.
Yesterday, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan) announced that there was to be mediation in the postal strike. I am glad of that and all of us in this House are glad of that. We hope it works and that they reach a negotiated settlement. I see the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) is present tonight and I am sure he would like to see a negotiated settlement so that he may enjoy a few days' rest.
But the Minister of Labour said that they cannot operate in mediation when we are looking over their shoulders. Mr. Speaker, every time this government goes to mediation, does that mean we have to close the House? Can we not operate and discuss other important bills? Just the other day the government House leader was telling everyone that there are 25 important pieces of legislation to be passed. We are prepared to discuss those while the mediation talks go on, but the government wants to get away. Hon. members opposite want to go on holidays. They got their pay raise, as we all did, but we are willing to stay here and work for it while they want to go off for the summer.
I see the chairman of the Quebec caucus hollering and hooting over there. I never see him on his feet. He always speaks from the seat of his pants. He does not have enough nerve to stand up. He is sitting on his best part.
I heard the Liberals say today that they cannot get the work of the House done. I have attended many committees, Mr. Speaker, where Liberals did not show up and it was not possible to have a quorum and carry on the meetings. I know why. All those guys on the back bench were putting pressure
July 17, 1981

on the cabinet for a number of things, one of which was a summer holiday. They finally won. They fought the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) and the government House leader (Mr. Pinard) into closing the place down for the summer. That is a shame and it is disgusting.
We do not have postal service in this country, inflation is running rampant, energy prices are going up and people are suffering under the detrimental effects of a non-caring government and a cabinet that has hardly been here the last couple of weeks. They have been on holidays already.
What has Jack Austin got on you guys?

Mr. Speaker, listen to hon. members over there. It is now three minutes past one. I get my full 20 minutes but they are calling for the vote now. They are in a real rush to get out of here. I am going to use my full 20 minutes. Let us take a look at the increased cost of energy. Since this government has been in power, it has raised the price of gasoline 13 times. In the province of Ontario it costs around SI.60 per gallon. I have listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) tell me they want another small piece of the pie. That is all they want. Right now, out of $1.60 per gallon the federal government gets 58 cents which is about 33 per cent. Now the federal government wants more. It is sad that most of the government's 33 per cent take is shipped out of the country to Saudi Arabia, Venezuela and Mexico.
And Brampton.
I wish it were shipped to Brampton, we could use it in Brampton. We could use mail delivery in Brampton, too.
Hear, hear!

Not only mail delivery when the Post Office is supposedly working, but some of those new subdivisions that have not had mail delivery for two years. They deserve it as well. What does the Postmaster General say? He tells people not to worry because when the Post Office becomes a Crown corporation, it will take care of them. I hope he is right because he has been telling that to everyone over here. He has been saying that the Crown corporation will solve all the problems of the Post Office. He has been putting a great deal of pressure on Michael Warren. I hope the Postmaster General is right, although I doubt it.
Do you want to stay next week?
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown has the floor.
Summer Recess

We will sit next week. Hon. members opposite are the ones who are closing the place down. You want to stop the work of the House.
I want to get back to the price of energy because I think this government has been hoodwinking the peopie of Canada. I want the Prime Minister who is not here and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who is not here, to explain to the Canadian people why they want more and more of the energy pie. This government already takes 33 per cent. How much more does the government want?
All of it.

That is right.
The Prime Minister likes to call all the backbenchers nobodies. The reason he does that is that he does not give them an opportunity to speak. Nobody can speak in this House. Any time there is an important issue, the Prime Minister invokes closure. I know the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) is as embarrassed as anyone over there by the closures which have been brought in on at least two very important issues. This issue is as important as the Constitution and the energy discussions. What does this cynical government do? It appoints a backbencher to the Senate who has served in this House for a relatively short period of time. Then that cute little cherub from the Prime Minister's office is parachuted into Spadina because he could not get elected in Alberta, the province from where he comes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He won't get elected in Spadina either.
I tell you now we are going to put the boots to Coutts.
Hear, hear!

I see them all laughing over there. They think the great annointed from the Prime Minister's office, the laying on of the hands, is going to walk right in. Now I hear leather lungs from Newfoundland hollering. This is bothering them. They know this was a bad move. First, members over there are very upset at the Senate appointment. I see a hundred people over there who deserve it more than the one who got it-maybe not a hundred.
At least the Liberals will have somebody with sex appeal now.
We are going to win Spadina. We have a terrific candidate in the person of Laura Sabia. You can all smirk over there but wait until August 17.
She will finish third.
Mr. Coutts will be back here. One of you lucky guys may get him as an assistant.

Maybe even a secretary.

July 17, 1981
Summer Recess
I shouldn't tell you that because it will probably encourage you to work to get him elected.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: All those in favour of the motion will please say yea.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I wish to draw to the attention of the hon. member that his remarks should be addressed to the Chair.
Yea.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: All those opposed will please say nay.

Through the Chair, Mr. Speaker, we are going to put the boots to Coutts.
To sum up, we on this side are very disappointed. We have had a session where we have seen closure brought in three times on three of the major issues facing this country today. The small businessmen in my community, many of them whose cash flow has been cut to under 50 per cent, who are carrying stock at 22 per cent at the bank who cannot afford any more loans to pay their staff and are laying them off while this government says "go away, do not worry about it, if we need you, we will call you back. There is no emergency now."
There is an emergency in this country. It is a very serious one. It is called a postal strike and we have to solve it and solve it quickly.
We are prepared to sit here and discuss all the government business. Bring on the bills. I say to the government House leader, bring on the 25 government bills and we will debate them while mediation goes on. We want to stay here to be assured that the postal strike is solved this summer.
The little pink rump to my left is nattering away. We know that the government has a majority and that it is going to put the padlock on this place until October 14. It really does not care about what is going on in this country. It wants to get away from here because the heat is too much. They are getting out of the kitchen. They do not like the heat of the uranium cartel. There are too many things that are bothering them.
The government doesn't like the pressure with regard to VIA Rail. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) should be ashamed with what is going on with VIA Rail. It is disgusting. The government does not like to see interest rates around 20 to 22 per cent. It does not like questions about what it is going to do about it. The government does not like questions about what it is going to do about people living in AHOP developments who are being kicked out because they cannot go from an 8 per cent mortgage to an 18 per cent first, plus a second mortgage to pay back the loan that the government so graciously made to them in the first place.

speechtext: On a point of order, Madam Speaker. As we are breaking now for a long period of time I wonder if it might be appropriate if I express, on behalf of all members of the House, our thanks to all members of the staff-security, pages, officers at the table, the Hansard staff, and all of those who have served us so well and so faithfully and who have done their best to make our life here as comfortable as possible.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, may I join the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton in the expression of good will which he
Summer Recess
has conveyed? 1 should like to add to those whom he has mentioned others who have served us-the press, who cover us in one way of another-
Boo!

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
I referred to the press who have covered us in one way or another.
Finally, special greetings to Your Honour.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, besides those who have been mentioned by my colleagues from Nepean Carleton (Mr. Baker) and my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I should like to thank our pages who acquired quite an exceptional experience and who have been very useful to us. I wish to pay them tribute.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On behalf of the government, we should also like to thank all the press people who have to adjust their schedule to ours, as well as the families of all parliamentarians and all those whose work is related to that of the House, for their patience and understanding in the circumstances.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I wish everyone a very happy holiday. I rejoice in the thought that their families will recuperate them. They must have thought they had lost them for all summer.
1 also want to say goodbye to our pages who are just as sad to leave us as we are to see them go.

Have a nice holiday and may God be with you.
At 1.44 a.m. the House adjourned until Wednesday, October 14, 1981 at 2 p.m.
